content: The use of tetracycline-class drugs during tooth development (the last half of pregnancy, infancy, and childhood up to the age of 8 years) can result in permanent discoloration of the teeth, presenting as yellow, gray, or brown staining. This adverse effect is more commonly observed with prolonged use of the drug but has also been reported following repeated short-term courses. Additionally, enamel hypoplasia has been documented. Therefore, tetracycline drugs should not be used in this age group unless alternative drugs are ineffective or contraindicated. Tetracyclines form a stable calcium complex in bone-forming tissues. A reduction in fibula growth rate has been observed in premature infants receiving oral tetracycline at doses of 25 mg/kg every six hours. This effect was shown to be reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. Animal studies indicate that tetracyclines cross the placenta, accumulate in fetal tissues, and may exert toxic effects on the developing fetus, often associated with delayed skeletal development. Evidence of embryotoxicity has also been noted in animals treated early in pregnancy. If tetracycline is used during pregnancy or if a patient becomes pregnant while taking the drug, the patient should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. Tetracycline drugs should only be used during pregnancy if absolutely necessary. In patients with renal impairment, even standard oral or parenteral doses may lead to excessive systemic accumulation of the drug, potentially resulting in liver toxicity. In such cases, lower total doses are recommended, and serum drug levels should be monitored if therapy is prolonged. Photosensitivity, characterized by an exaggerated sunburn reaction, has been reported in some individuals taking tetracyclines. Patients who are likely to be exposed to direct sunlight or ultraviolet light should be warned about this potential reaction. Treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of skin erythema. The anti-anabolic effects of tetracyclines may cause an increase in blood urea nitrogen (BUN). While this is not typically an issue in individuals with normal renal function, patients with significantly impaired renal function may experience azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, and acidosis due to elevated serum tetracycline levels. As with other antibiotics, the use of tetracycline may result in the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. If superinfection occurs, the antibiotic should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Infections caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci should be treated for at least ten days. Bulging fontanels in infants and benign intracranial hypertension in adults have been reported in individuals receiving tetracyclines. These conditions resolved upon discontinuation of the drug. When indicated, surgical procedures such as incision and drainage should be performed alongside antibiotic therapy. Prescribing tetracycline in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including tetracycline, should only be used to treat bacterial infections. When prescribed for a bacterial infection, patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or failing to complete the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance, rendering tetracycline or other antibacterial drugs ineffective in the future. In cases of venereal diseases where coexistent syphilis is suspected, dark-field examinations should be performed before starting treatment, and blood serology should be repeated monthly for at least four months. For long-term therapy, periodic laboratory evaluations of organ systems, including hematopoietic, renal, and hepatic studies, should be conducted. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillin, so concurrent use with penicillin or other bactericidal antibiotics should be avoided. Tetracyclines have been shown to depress plasma prothrombin activity, and patients on anticoagulant therapy may require a downward adjustment of their anticoagulant dosage. Concurrent use of tetracycline and methoxyflurane has been reported to result in fatal renal toxicity. The absorption of tetracyclines is impaired by antacids containing aluminum, calcium, or magnesium, as well as preparations containing iron, zinc, or sodium bicarbonate. Concurrent use of tetracycline may also reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives. Long-term animal studies are being conducted to determine whether tetracycline hydrochloride has carcinogenic potential. Some related antibiotics, such as oxytetracycline and minocycline, have shown evidence of oncogenic activity in rats. In two in vitro mammalian cell assay systems (L5178Y mouse lymphoma and Chinese hamster lung cells), mutagenicity was observed at tetracycline hydrochloride concentrations of 60 and 10 mcg/mL, respectively. Tetracycline hydrochloride did not affect fertility when administered in the diet to male and female rats at a daily intake of 25 times the human dose. Pregnant women with renal disease may be more susceptible to tetracycline-associated liver failure. The effects of tetracyclines on labor and delivery are unknown. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made whether to discontinue the drug, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother. For pediatric use, refer to the warnings and dosage and administration guidelines.
